fixes.explanation: Light it is, friend. The Teacher says "…wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness…" (Ecclesiastes 2:13). He looks at wisdom and folly side by side and gives wisdom the win. It's like flipping on the kitchen light and finally seeing where the cookie sheet actually is.

Close, but the Teacher says the opposite here, friend. He says the wise man has eyes in his head and the fool walks in darkness. Then he adds, "Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both." (Ecclesiastes 2:14). One fate, not two, so the wise man and the fool do not end up with different fates.

False is right, friend. The Teacher first says the wise man has eyes in his head and the fool walks in darkness. Then comes the turn: "Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both." (Ecclesiastes 2:14). The wise man and the fool end up with the same fate, not different ones. I bet that gave him plenty to think about.

You'd think a wise man would just study harder, wouldn't you? But that's not the question he asks. He says, "What then have I gained by being wise?" (Ecclesiastes 2:15). He turns his question back on the wisdom he already has.

Praise would be nice, but that's not what the Teacher says. He says "…there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come." (Ecclesiastes 2:16). No lasting remembrance, for the wise or for the fool. Praise isn't in the verse at all.

He did, friend. The Teacher says plainly, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). That's a heavy thing to say, and I think it hurts to read. The reason he gives is that the work done under the sun was grievous to him.

The Teacher goes the other direction, baker. He says, "So I hated life…" (Ecclesiastes 2:17). The reason he gives is that the work done under the sun was grievous to him. Loving life even more isn't in the verse.

That's it, baker. He says, "…I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me." (Ecclesiastes 2:17). The work itself weighed on him. Then he adds, "For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind." (Ecclesiastes 2:17).
No battle in this verse, baker. The Teacher gives this reason: "…I must leave it to the man who comes after me." (Ecclesiastes 2:18). That's why he hated all he had toiled for. Battle never comes up.

False is right, baker. The Teacher says, "…my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun." (Ecclesiastes 2:20). Despair, not peace. So the verse says the opposite of finding peace.

Evil is the word, friend. When a man who labored with wisdom, knowledge and skill must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it, the Teacher says "…this too is futile and a great evil." (Ecclesiastes 2:21). He puts that label on it himself. I think it's a hard verse to read.

Mystery sounds gentler, baker, but that's not his word. He says a man's portion going to someone who has not worked for it is "…futile and a great evil." (Ecclesiastes 2:21). I think he's bothered by it. Still, the word he actually uses is evil.
Mind it is, baker. The Teacher says, "…even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Even at night, the mind keeps going. The verse names the mind as what does not rest.

You'd think tired hands would finally get a rest, friend. But the verse says, "…even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). Hands aren't mentioned there. It's the mind that does not rest.
His household isn't mentioned in this verse, baker. The Teacher says, "…even at night, his mind does not rest." (Ecclesiastes 2:23). The trouble named is his mind. It isn't the people around him.

Gathering isn't what he calls better, baker. He says, "Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work." (Ecclesiastes 2:24). Piling up more isn't part of that. Enjoying the work is.

Yes, baker. The text says, "…to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God." (Ecclesiastes 2:26). The sinner gathers, and what he gathers is handed over to one who pleases God. That's the task the Teacher names for the sinner, set beside the wisdom, knowledge and joy God gives the one who pleases Him.
